title: Is It Normal for Your Interests to Completely Change?
metaTitle: Is It Normal for Your Interests to Completely Change?
metaDescription: Yes — interests and tastes shift across life, and people reliably underestimate how much they'll change. What the research suggests about evolving preferences.
keyFinding: Interests and tastes commonly shift across life, and research suggests people systematically underestimate how much their preferences will keep changing in the future.
honestAnswer: Yes, it is normal — and more expected than most people realise. The research on how preferences change over a lifetime suggests that interests, values, and tastes keep evolving with experience and life stage, while some kinds of taste tend to settle early. Outgrowing things you once loved, and being drawn to things that once held no appeal, is a common feature of moving through life rather than a sign that something has gone wrong.

One of the more striking findings is that people are generally poor at predicting this about themselves. We tend to feel that who we are now is more or less who we will stay, even though our own past shows we have changed a great deal. So the experience of your interests shifting can feel surprising even when, statistically, it is the ordinary path.
whatDataShows: A widely cited study by Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson (2013, Science) described what they called the 'End of History Illusion': across thousands of participants of different ages, people consistently underestimated how much their personalities, values, and preferences would change over the next decade — even though, looking back, they readily acknowledged how much they had changed over the previous one. People at every age seemed to believe they had just now arrived at the person they would remain.

Not all tastes are equally fluid, though. Research on musical taste suggests it largely crystallises in adolescence and early adulthood, with the music people are exposed to in those years tending to anchor their preferences for life. So some interests do appear to set relatively young, while broader interests, hobbies, and values seem to keep shifting with new experiences and circumstances.

Personality offers a related clue. The Big Five trait of Openness to experience — closely linked to curiosity and appetite for novelty — tends to be higher in young adulthood and decline gently across the lifespan on average. But 'on average' hides wide individual variation, and meaningful change continues at every age rather than stopping at some fixed point.
whyItFeelsDifferent: Changing interests can feel destabilising because we tend to treat our current self as the finished version. The End of History Illusion captures this neatly: at any age, we feel we have essentially arrived, which makes a later shift in what we care about feel like a deviation rather than a continuation of a pattern we have followed all along.

There is also a sunk-cost dimension. If you invested years, money, or identity in an interest — a career path, a hobby, a community built around it — losing the pull toward it can feel like a loss or even a betrayal of your past self, rather than the natural movement of preferences over time.

And because the tastes that do set early, like music, feel so stable, we can over-generalise and expect all our interests to be equally permanent. When the more fluid ones change, the contrast can make the shift feel more alarming than it is.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most useful takeaway from this research is simply to expect change rather than be ambushed by it. If people reliably underestimate how much they will shift, then building in the assumption that your interests will keep evolving tends to make the eventual change feel less like a crisis.

Holding your current identity a little more loosely appears to help. Since the evidence suggests preferences are a moving target, treating 'this is just who I am and what I like' as provisional rather than fixed leaves more room to follow new curiosity without feeling you have failed at the old one.

It can also help to give yourself explicit permission to outgrow things. The data frames dropping an old interest not as quitting or flakiness but as a normal feature of a developing life — closer to the rule than the exception.
whatDoesNotHelp: Forcing yourself to stay loyal to an old interest purely because it once defined you tends not to help, and the research on changing preferences gives little reason to treat past taste as an obligation. Persisting out of identity rather than genuine pull rarely rekindles the original interest.

Treating a shift in interests as evidence of a deeper problem — instability, lack of commitment, not knowing yourself — is usually a misreading. The End of History findings suggest that change is the norm across the whole population, so reading it as a personal flaw misattributes an ordinary process.

Assuming the new interest will, by contrast, be permanent is also a predictable trap. The same illusion that made you think the old self was final will tend to make the current self feel final too. Expecting further change is more accurate than expecting to have finally settled.
realNumbersInContext: The clearest signal here is not a single statistic but a robust pattern: across a very large sample spanning ages roughly 18 to 68, Quoidbach and colleagues (2013) found people at every age predicted they would change far less in the next ten years than people ten years older reported having actually changed. The gap held for values, preferences, and personality alike — a consistent underestimation of one's own future change.

Set against that, the crystallisation of musical taste in adolescence and early adulthood is a useful counterweight: it shows that some preferences do anchor young while others stay fluid. And the gentle average decline in Openness across adulthood is exactly that — gentle and average, with wide individual differences and continued change at all ages, not a hard stop on developing new interests.

faqs.question: Is it normal to lose interest in hobbies I used to love?
faqs.answer: Yes. Research on how preferences change suggests interests keep evolving with experience and life stage, so outgrowing an old hobby is a common part of a developing life rather than a sign of instability. Some tastes set early, but many stay fluid throughout adulthood.

faqs.question: Why do my interests change but my taste in music doesn't?
faqs.answer: Studies suggest musical taste largely crystallises in adolescence and early adulthood and then stays relatively stable, while broader interests and values tend to keep shifting. It is normal for different kinds of preference to change at very different rates.

faqs.question: Does my personality changing mean my interests will too?
faqs.answer: Often, yes — they are related. The trait of Openness, linked to curiosity and appetite for novelty, tends to be highest in young adulthood and decline gently on average. But change continues at every age, and individual variation is wide, so there is no fixed point where your interests stop developing.

faqs.question: Will my current interests last this time?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but it is worth holding the assumption loosely. The 'End of History Illusion' shows people at every age expect to change little going forward, yet keep changing anyway. Expecting your interests to keep evolving tends to be more accurate than assuming you have finally settled.

faqs.question: Am I flaky for switching interests so often?
faqs.answer: The research reframes this. Because changing preferences appears to be the norm across the whole population, frequent shifts in interest are better understood as ordinary development than as flakiness or a failure to commit.
